raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that typically manifests during the last month of pregnancy or in the early postpartum months, in the absence of any other identifiable cause of heart failure [1, 2]. First comprehensively described over half a century ago [1], PPCM represents a distinct clinical entity with a global, though highly variable, distribution [3]. While the incidence in the United States is estimated at approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births [4], regions such as Haiti [5] and parts of Africa experience a significantly higher burden, with rates as high as 1 in 100 live births in certain areas [3, 5, 6]. Known maternal risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, African ancestry, multiple gestations, and crucially, preeclampsia and other gestational hypertensive disorders, which are present in over 20% of PPCM patients [7].

Over the past two decades, translational research has unveiled a vascular-hormonal paradigm at the core of PPCM pathogenesis. Late in pregnancy and early postpartum, a state of elevated oxidative stress triggers the proteolytic cleavage of the nursing hormone prolactin by cathepsin D, yielding a toxic 16-kDa prolactin fragment [8]. This fragment is highly anti-angiogenic, pro-apoptotic, and pro-inflammatory, inducing endothelial cell damage, capillary dissociation, and downstream cardiomyocyte dysfunction [8, 9]. Simultaneously, late-pregnancy elevations in placenta-derived soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1)—a potent vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) antagonist—contribute to systemic endothelial dysfunction, highlighting the mechanistic overlap between PPCM and preeclampsia [9]. Genetic studies further indicate that PPCM is not purely idiopathic but frequently shares a genetic landscape with familial dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [10]. Truncating variants in the titin gene (*TTN*) are detected in up to 10% to 15% of PPCM patients, suggesting that gestational stress unmasks a latent genetic predisposition [11]. Downstream, molecular markers like microRNA-146a [12], interferon-gamma (IFN-$\gamma$) [13], and placental growth factor (PlGF) [14] play crucial roles as mediators and potential biomarkers of this disease process.

The clinical presentation of PPCM spans from subacute heart failure symptoms, such as dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea, to catastrophic cardiogenic shock and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [15]. Given that many early symptoms overlap with normal physiological changes of late pregnancy, diagnosis is often dangerously delayed [15]. Diagnostic evaluation hinges on echocardiographic confirmation of left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45% [16]. Expert position statements emphasize early screening using electrocardiography, natriuretic peptides, and echocardiography to ensure prompt recognition and treatment [16, 17].

Management of PPCM follows standard guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure, with critical modifications based on gestational status [17, 18]. During pregnancy, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) are strictly contraindicated due to fetotoxicity and must be replaced with alternative vasodilators like hydralazine and nitrates [17, 18]. Beta-blockers, loop diuretics, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are standard postpartum [18]. 

A unique target of therapy is prolactin suppression. The dopamine agonist bromocriptine has emerged as a disease-modifying agent [19, 20]. Clinical registries and randomized trials demonstrate that adding bromocriptine to standard GDMT significantly enhances LVEF recovery and improves clinical outcomes [20, 21]. Suppressing lactation requires parallel consideration of infant feeding and requires prophylactic anticoagulation due to the elevated thromboembolic risk associated with both PPCM and bromocriptine [22]. For patients presenting with refractory cardiogenic shock, temporary mechanical circulatory support (such as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation or left ventricular assist devices) acts as a critical bridge to recovery or transplantation [23]. Furthermore, because patients with severely reduced LVEF are at high risk of sudden cardiac death, the temporary use of a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) is strongly recommended during the initial 3 to 6 months of therapy optimization [24].

While PPCM carries significant morbidity, it displays a higher rate of myocardial recovery than other cardiomyopathies, with approximately 50% to 70% of patients recovering normal LV function within six months postpartum [25]. However, prognosis varies globally; long-term survival is significantly lower in regions with limited access to care [26]. A subsequent pregnancy carries a substantial risk of recurrence, estimated at up to 20% in women who have completely recovered their LVEF, and over 50% in those with persistent LV dysfunction, where future pregnancy is strongly contraindicated [27, 28]. Safe care in future gestations requires multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric surveillance, and reliable postpartum contraception is a vital aspect of long-term management [29]. In conclusion, a deep understanding of PPCM's molecular mechanisms, early diagnosis, and targeted therapeutic interventions remain key to improving outcomes for afflicted mothers globally [30].
